Treacherously
TRECH-ur-us-lee
adv. (faithlessly, in violation of covenant; rendering the Hebrew verb bagad)
From Old French trecherie, trickery, from trechier, to cheat. In the KJV it almost always renders one Hebrew verb, bagad, whose noun means a garment — the treacherous man covers himself, and Malachi plays on exactly that image.

Biblical Definition

To deal treacherously is to break faith with one to whom you were bound, and the word belongs to covenant rather than to ordinary dishonesty. Its densest use is Malachi's indictment of easy divorce, where the prophet answers a congregation that cannot understand why God ignores its offerings: “the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, against whom thou hast dealt treacherously: yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant” (Malachi 2:14). Marriage is here a covenant with God as witness, which is why its breach is treachery and not merely unkindness; and the chapter closes with a warning aimed at the inner man: “take heed to your spirit, that ye deal not treacherously” (Malachi 2:16). The same verb makes marital unfaithfulness the model for Israel's idolatry: “Surely as a wife treacherously departeth from her husband, so have ye dealt treacherously with me, O house of Israel, saith the LORD” (Jeremiah 3:20). And Isaiah piles the root on itself in a cry of exhaustion at a world where faithlessness has become the norm — “the treacherous dealers have dealt treacherously; yea, the treacherous dealers have dealt very treacherously” (Isaiah 24:16). The repetition is the point. Treachery is the sin that destroys the possibility of any other dealing, because it attacks the trust every other transaction stands on.

Webster 1828 Definition

Faithlessly, in breach of covenant. Malachi makes it the verdict on divorce, with God as witness to the marriage; Jeremiah makes marital treachery the pattern of idolatry; Isaiah repeats the root four times in a single verse of grief.

expand to see more

TREACHEROUSLY, adv. By violating allegiance or faith pledged; by betraying a trust; faithlessly; perfidiously.

2. In a manner to betray; as, he dealt treacherously with his companion.

TREACHEROUS, a. [Fr. trecheur, a cheat.] Violating allegiance or faith pledged; false; faithless.

3. Betraying or discovering a trust reposed; as a treacherous friend.

4. In Scripture, applied to breach of the marriage covenant and of covenant with God. Mal. 2.

Key Scripture

Malachi 2:14 — "Yet ye say, Wherefore? Because the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, against whom thou hast dealt treacherously: yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant."

Malachi 2:16 — "For the LORD, the God of Israel, saith that he hateth putting away: for one covereth violence with his garment, saith the LORD of hosts: therefore take heed to your spirit, that ye deal not treacherously."

Jeremiah 3:20 — "Surely as a wife treacherously departeth from her husband, so have ye dealt treacherously with me, O house of Israel, saith the LORD."

Isaiah 24:16 — "From the uttermost part of the earth have we heard songs, even glory to the righteous. But I said, My leanness, my leanness, woe unto me! the treacherous dealers have dealt treacherously; yea, the treacherous dealers have dealt very treacherously."

Modern Corruption

Malachi 2:16 is softened or re-punctuated until it no longer says that God hates putting away, and the covenant frame that makes divorce treachery rather than misfortune is replaced by the language of two people growing apart.

expand to see more

The plain sense of Malachi 2:16 in the Authorized Version is that the LORD hates putting away — hates the act of divorce — and the surrounding verses supply the reason: He was the witness at the wedding, and He counts its dissolution a breach of covenant against a companion. That has proved an unwelcome verse, and a good deal of ingenuity has been spent on making it say something else, most often by recasting it as a condemnation only of the man who divorces treacherously rather than of putting away as such. The dictionary keeps the received text and reads Malachi with the Lord Jesus, who takes the same ground in Matthew 19:4-9: from the beginning it was not so, what God has joined man is not to sunder, and the single exception granted is for fornication. That is neither the absolute prohibition of Rome nor the elastic permission of the age.

Underneath the exegetical dispute lies a change of category that costs more. When a marriage ends, modern speech supplies vocabulary in which no one has done anything: the relationship ran its course, the parties grew apart, it was no longer fulfilling. Bagad names an agent and a victim — someone dealt treacherously, and someone was dealt with. Malachi's congregation was genuinely baffled by God's displeasure and asked wherefore?, which is exactly the response the covenant frame produces when it has been forgotten. The recovery is not a harsher tone toward the divorced, many of whom were the ones betrayed, but the restoration of the frame: marriage is a covenant sworn before a Witness who does not forget the terms.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew bagad (to act covertly, deal treacherously, break faith), related to beged, a garment or covering — the treacherous man conceals himself, and Malachi 2:16 turns the pun on covering violence with a garment.

expand to see more

Hebrew bagad (H898) — to act treacherously, deal faithlessly; the verb in Malachi 2:14-16, Jeremiah 3:20, and Isaiah 24:16.

Hebrew beged (H899) — a garment, covering; the cognate noun, and the image behind covering violence with a garment.

Hebrew bogedim — the treacherous dealers; the participle repeated for effect in Isaiah 24:16 and Jeremiah 12:1.

Hebrew berith (H1285) — covenant; the bond whose breach makes the dealing treacherous rather than merely unkind.

Greek asynthetos (G802) — covenant-breakers; the Septuagint and Pauline equivalent, listed in Romans 1:31.

Usage

"“The wife of thy covenant” — the phrase that makes divorce a covenant breach and not a private disappointment."

"“Take heed to your spirit, that ye deal not treacherously” — the guard is set on the inner man before the act."

"“The treacherous dealers have dealt very treacherously” — Isaiah's cry at a society where faithlessness has become ordinary."
